blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State what supply means, show it as a supply schedule and curve, and tell supply apart from demand.

blocks.heading: The definition of supply
blocks.text: Supply is the quantity of a good that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period of time. Two parts must both hold. The producer must be willing to sell at that price, and able to offer the good: with stock, capacity or the right to sell it. A fisher in Walvis Bay who would like to sell horse mackerel at N$20 a kilogram but has no catch that week is not supplying at that price; a wish to sell without the ability to offer stays outside supply.

blocks.heading: From schedule to curve
blocks.text: A producer that writes down the quantity it would offer at each price has drawn up a supply schedule. Marula Foods of Gobabis dries marula fruit for shops across Namibia: at N$20 a packet it offers 300 packets a month, at N$30 it offers 450 packets, at N$40 it offers 600 packets. Drawn as a diagram, the price per packet goes on the vertical axis and the packets a month on the horizontal, and the supply curve slopes upward through the three points. A rose grower in the Netherlands books the same upward relationship for bunches sold at auction. The curve as a whole is supply itself, not any single point on it.

blocks.heading: Sellers or buyers
blocks.text: The confusion learners make: supply and demand are mixed up, because both describe a quantity at a price. The boundary: supply belongs to the sellers - the quantity producers are willing and able to offer - while demand, from topic 2.3, belongs to the buyers - the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy. The test: ask whose decision sets the quantity. Where a firm chooses how much to put on its shelf, the quantity is supply; where a household chooses how much to take home, it is demand.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 2.3 drew the buying half of the market; this topic draws the selling half, and topic 2.5 brings the two together to fix the market price.
